I tell people over and over that it's never enough to simply read the abstract and/or the conclusions section of a peer-reviewed paper. The only way to assess the claims of the author(s) is to objectively examine the data for yourself and see if you'd come to the same conclusions. This applies not only to social "science" papers, but also to other fields (chemistry, medicine, etc) which are considered "hard" sciences. (See this for the case in medicine).

People seem to think that academia is somehow impervious to dishonesty and to people who are willing to get ahead by any means necessary, up to and including lying about your work in order to get published, or become famous, or to push your agenda, or to confirm and try to prove your worldview to others. It's been my experience that only a handful of social "science" papers I've read have conclusion that I'd agree with after reading their methods and results. Even the ones whose conclusions "agree" with my worldview (something that's harder and harder to find) are suspect in some manner. Sadly, I'd say about half of the biochem & neurobio papers I've read have a similar problem.

In short, you don't need to be an academic or an expert in some field in order to read and objectively assess the claims in the latest "scientific study" that has the media's panties in a twist. Just ask questions from a skeptical point of view. The OP video brought up a great question: how did you get all that data from around the world? If an author doesn't present their data, it's probably bullshit. Be similarly inquisitive when you read a paper claiming that, say, students feel X because of Y. Ask, "how did they come to find out people's innermost, buried feelings?" Look at their data. Say you find in their methods that they simply gave a group of university students a questionnaire. (With EdPsy studies, this is how they gather data 90% of the time.) Then ask, "can I see the questions?" (50% of the time you can't, the other 50% you'll find that it's not easy to obtain the ACTUAL questions they ask...if not impossible.) Put yourself in a student's shoes and ask, "if I were asked these questions, would I be 100% honest, or might I lie -- even to myself, even though the test is "anonymous" -- in order to save face and not to damage my own self-image?" Finally, see if the authors are extrapolating their results too far. In the example above, they've asked a group of university students 5 questions and came to the conclusion that "students feel X because of Y." Are they trying to apply this "result" to high school students? To primary students? Were the questionnaires given to fellow EdPsy students? Did they bother to question any engineering students? Physicists? (Most the time this data is not available.) Are they making a claim about a wide body of people after only gathering data about a very small group with shared interests? (You'd be disgusted to learn how often this is the case in the education field.)

Please keep in mind (and help others to understand) that "scientists" are not immune to lying, cheating, and trying to get ahead by misrepresenting their results. When people's careers and worldviews and lifetimes of research are on the line, they -- no matter how "objective" their field claims itself to be -- can convince even themselves of the truth of their idea, and then doctor their representation of the data in order to fit to that idea.
